rationale:
The experience register exists to hold user-experience contracts specific enough to be machine-checked. Its central clause — the `no-inert-control` invariant, 'a control that cannot do anything must not be presented as a control' — arrived in six independent implementations across two sites and five authors, and is the reason the workstream was started. It has never been checkable. Measured 2026-07-28 across the nine harvested entries: attribute assertion blocks 13 of the 38 deferred clauses and there is no entry it does not affect. Six entries had already AUTHORED attribute checks (8 of them) before any of this code existed, and the write-time validator refused every one as 'not executable by any tier'. So the register can record the rule it was built to enforce and cannot run it. The approval council's verdict on the first entry (corr ec91c7e4) made this the blocking objection, twice, at [high]. This change implements the two check types the entries had already agreed on, at Tier 2, and nothing else. It is deliberately the SMALLEST thing that closes that gap: no new bindings, no planner work, no lifecycle change.

SCOPE DECLARATION, because this is a shared-vocabulary addition and the 2026-07-28 owner ruling on platform seams applies. `evaluateStaticCriteria` is the one Tier 2 evaluator, shared by tool acceptance and (through the exported door) by the experience register. Adding a check type widens a vocabulary every criteria document draws on. Blast radius MEASURED, not argued (per the ruling that '"no collision is possible" is a query, not an argument'): 78 criteria fences exist in doc_plans fleet-wide; 0 of them contain `attribute_absent`, 0 contain `attribute_matches`; 1 experience_patterns row does (CC-001, ours). Both types previously fell to the switch's `default:` branch and were SKIPPED, so no existing document changes outcome — the new cases are reachable only by a document that opts in by naming the type, and today exactly one does. There is NO ordering constraint claimed here and this is not being smuggled ahead of review: the change is being submitted before it ships, and the reviewers are asked to judge the scope question squarely.

THE DESIGN DECISION THAT MATTERS is what happens when the selector matches nothing. This is not a detail: for a list whose rows are cloned client-side, zero matched elements is the NORMAL Tier 2 state, and 'no inert row carries a dead href' is then vacuously true. A pass there would be the register committing the exact defect it exists to end. A failure there would call a correct page broken — which is what this workstream actually did on 2026-07-28, producing its first verdict ('broken') about a page that was fine, by executing a check it had already recorded as impossible. So zero matches SKIPS: reported, never counted, and unable to satisfy `experienceVerdict`, which requires at least one PASS and zero FAILS.

plan.summary: The Tier 2 static criteria evaluator cannot assert anything about an element's ATTRIBUTES, so the experience register's central rule — a control that cannot act must not be presented as one — is recorded and never checked. Eight attribute checks authored across six register entries are all refused at write time as unexecutable. This adds `attribute_absent` and `attribute_matches` to the Tier 2 evaluator in the shape those entries already use, teaches the register's validator that they are now executable, and refuses at write time an attribute check that would assert nothing. Zero matched elements SKIPS rather than passing vacuously or failing a correct page. Proven against six live pages: 6 checks PASS over 18 real elements, 1 correctly SKIPS, 1 FAILS on a genuine served `href="#"`.

edits.rationale: The evaluation itself, in a file of its own so the shared evaluator's diff stays small and the new capability is reviewable in one place. Attribute assertion is the only check that needs element IDENTITY rather than presence, so it is the only one that parses a DOM (goquery, already a direct dependency). The two selector semantics coexist safely because the DOM selector is strictly STRICTER than the existing anchor rule: anything it matches, the anchor rule would also have matched, so it can never pass something the anchor rule would fail. The selector is compiled explicitly with cascadia rather than handed to goquery.Find, because Find returns an empty selection for a MALFORMED selector — which would make a typo in the criteria indistinguishable from the ordinary client-side-rendering case, and those two need opposite answers.

Route the two new types to the DOM path and give the decode struct the four fields the register's entries already author. The DOM is parsed lazily and at most once per evaluation, so every other check type keeps working on the raw string and pays nothing. The new `case` label is what the existing source-lockstep test reads, so the validator's capability table cannot silently disagree with this switch.
edits.sketch:
case "page_status_ok":
 			...
+		case "attribute_absent", "attribute_matches":
+			doc, err := pageDOM()   // lazy; parsed at most once per evaluation
+			if err != nil {
+				skip(ch.ID, "served page could not be parsed into a DOM: "+err.Error())
+				break
+			}
+			out := evaluateAttributeCheck(doc, ch)
+			switch out.verdict {
+			case attrPass: pass(ch.ID, out.detail)
+			case attrFail: fail(ch.ID, out.detail)
+			default:       skip(ch.ID, out.detail)
+			}
 		default:
 
 type criteriaCheck struct {
 	...
+	Attributes []string `json:"attributes"`   // attribute_absent: none of these may be present
+	Attribute  string   `json:"attribute"`    // attribute_matches: the one attribute under test
+	Matches    string   `json:"matches"`      // value must match this regexp
+	NotMatches string   `json:"not_matches"`  // value must NOT match this regexp
 }

edits.rationale: Three things. (1) The capability table gains both types at Tier 2, which is what stops the validator refusing the entries' own checks and what makes verify_site_experience run them rather than hold them back — both consumers read this one table. (2) The new fields are declared PER TYPE rather than added to the global read-fields set: an `attributes` list means something on `attribute_absent` and nothing at all on `selector_exists`, and folding them together would stop rule P7 catching the second case, which is the exact 'field the runner never reads' defect P7 exists for. (3) A new rule P10 refuses at write time an attribute check that would assert nothing — no attributes listed, no attribute named, no pattern, or a pattern that does not compile. These are errors even when the check is marked deferred: deferral says the PLATFORM cannot run the check yet, it is not permission to store one that would be vacuous the day it can. The runner's honest response to such a check is a SKIP, which is silent; write time is the only loud moment.

A second lockstep, added because of a defect this workstream shipped four days ago: migration 259's guard compared my list against my own list and passed while the contract with the real consumer was broken. Both sides were mine, so it verified nothing. Here the other side is not mine and cannot be edited into agreement — a field the validator claims is read must have a json tag in a checker's own decode struct, because without one the runner literally cannot see it. Also replaces the now-false case in TestValidateExperienceCriteria_UnexecutableChecks, which used `attribute_absent` as its example of a type no tier executes; that gap is the one this change closes, so the case moves to `selector_text_empty` (the empty-region assertion, which the entries also author and which really is still beyond us) and the change is marked in the test's own comment rather than made silently.

Ten tests, and every HTML fixture is a verbatim element from a page fetched live on 2026-07-28 rather than markup written to suit the code. That is not decoration: this workstream invented a `contract` shape four days ago, tested it against fixtures it had also written, passed every test, and found that all nine real entries disagreed. The three guards were each proved by induced fault before submission — making zero-matches PASS fails two tests; claiming a per-type field no runner decodes fails the lockstep; folding the per-type fields into the global set fails the leak test.

grounded_in: Static checks CONFIRM, never refute: a runtime-built path passes on its anchor; only an absent anchor fails.

SKIPPED IS NOT PASSED. It is a separate list on purpose: a skipped check asserts nothing, and the failure this whole area keeps producing is a skip being read as a pass. Callers deciding "did this verify?" must require at least one PASSED and zero FAILED — never merely "no failures", which is also true of a document in which every check was skipped.
An entry WITHOUT one is NOT offered as openable: class --static, the template's placeholder href is REMOVED (it is href="#", a dead control), no tabindex, no handler.

The component's entire reason for existing — the openable/inert split — has zero executable coverage: both attribute_absent checks (no_dead_row_hrefs, template_row_not_a_control) are deferred, leaving list_exists as the only clean pass.
One rule: a control that cannot do anything must not be presented as a control. Six implementations, five of them written without reference to each other.
P7  a check carrying a field no checker reads is DEFERRED if it says so, an error if it does not
plan.risks:
MEASURED BLAST RADIUS, so a reviewer does not have to take it on trust: 78 criteria fences exist in doc_plans fleet-wide; `SELECT count(*) FROM doc_plans WHERE body LIKE '%attribute_absent%'` returns 0 and the same for attribute_matches; exactly 1 experience_patterns row uses either. Both types previously hit the switch's `default:` and were SKIPPED, so no existing document changes outcome.

WHAT A REVIEWER SHOULD CHECK, in the order I think they matter. (1) THE SCOPE QUESTION IS REAL AND I AM NOT ASSUMING THE ANSWER. This widens a vocabulary shared by every criteria document, which the 2026-07-28 owner ruling calls architecture-scope even when additive. I claim no ordering constraint and I am not asking for an exemption; I am asking whether a check type belongs in the seam class at all, given it is reachable only by opt-in. If the panel thinks it does, the right outcome is to route it to architecture review, not to approve it quickly. (2) TIER 2 NOW REFUTES, WHERE ITS STATED RULE IS 'CONFIRM, NEVER REFUTE'. My answer is that refutation is confined to elements actually present in the served HTML — anything JS builds matches nothing and skips — and that the precedent already exists in the same function, whose built-in `shell-dead-controls` sweep fails a page for a no-op href. A reviewer who disagrees should say so, because it is the one place this change alters the character of an existing mechanism rather than extending it. (3) THE SKIP-ON-ZERO RULE IS THE WHOLE SAFETY ARGUMENT and is one line; if it is ever 'simplified' to a pass, every attribute check in the register silently becomes vacuous. It is pinned by two tests and I probed it by induced fault. (4) A MISSING ATTRIBUTE FAILS rather than skips, which is a judgement, not a fact: I take it because a matched element that lacks the attribute the contract names is the strongest form of not matching, and skipping would make 'cards are links' green for a grid of divs. (5) goquery becomes a new import in discovery_checks (already a direct module dependency, used in four other platform files) and cascadia moves from indirect to direct in go.mod.

WHAT THIS CHANGE DOES NOT DO, stated so it is not read in: it does not re-seed any register entry, does not change any entry's status, does not touch the approval lifecycle, and does not alter `executable_checks` semantics. A separate and smaller defect — the validator counts a check carrying `tier: 4` as executable while the runner holds it back, so `executable_checks` overstates coverage — is deliberately NOT fixed here. It is a different change with a different argument and folding it in would be the 'accreted a second change during review' failure this workstream logged four days ago.

PROVEN AGAINST LIVE PAGES BEFORE SUBMISSION, not just unit tests. The eight authored checks were run through the real exported evaluator against six pages fetched today: CC-002 cta_has_real_destination PASS (1 element), CC-003 cards_have_real_destinations PASS (4), CC-004 cards_are_links PASS (6), CC-005 links_have_real_destinations PASS (2), CC-006 accessible_name_carries_the_real_figure PASS (4, aria-label), CC-007 link_if_present_is_real PASS (1); CC-001 no_dead_row_hrefs SKIP (rows are cloned client-side, so the selector matched nothing — the check correctly declined rather than passing vacuously); CC-001 template_row_not_a_control FAIL, on a genuinely served `<a class="provocations-archive__item" data-archive-template hidden href="#">`. That last one is a finding, not a regression: the component's own loader comment calls that href a dead control, but the page also carries `data-runtime-fill="true"`, which the platform's existing dead-control sweep treats as an exemption because such hrefs hydrate client-side. The two positions disagree. Resolving it belongs to the entry, not to this change — it is a question of which tier that clause is asserted at — and it is being handled in the register, not by weakening the check.
